Apps for devices that I purchased that show ads is probably one of my biggeset tech pet peeves.

My bank sends me emails that are ads for their other services but I guess if they mention my account and claim the email is for account purposes or something they get to claim it's not spam and I can't unsubscribe.
100%. I heavily leverage Gmail filters for this and it works very well most of the time.

Apple used to forbid marketing notifications, but they relaxed their policy a while ago.

What's really needed is system-wide notification channels, a hard requirement on app developers that marketing notifications go into the marketing channel, per-channel notification permissions, and a global off-switch for marketing channel notifications.

Apple needs to break this shitty business model. There's no incentive for Apple to keep allowing it.
They relaxed their policy because they themselves were doing it and it seemed too hypocritical even for them

Years ago, the combination of my forgetfulness and our urban address led to some thefts -- turns out, the garage is far more secure if you remember to close it.

I looked around for some kind of device that would close it automatically, which apparently doesn't exist -- with good reason, honestly. What I found was a weird little IoT box that functioned as a garage door opener, and which I could configure with an app on my phone to yell at us (via notifications) if we left the door open for more than 5 minutes.

An unsought side benefit that nevertheless became handy was that we could now control the garage door with our phones.

That app was, initially, pretty straightforward and clean -- but over time, fucking ADS crept in. I was about ready to shift platforms to avoid that crap when we moved across the country. We lived in our new place first in a rental while we house-hunted, so I did nothing there, but I absolutely planned to find an ad-free owner-respecting platform for my garage needs in the new house.

Except, well, the house we bought had (has) a pretty dang new opener, and it's delightfully almost-silent, and it has the MyQ stuff built in already. So I'm right back where I started, cursing these craven weasels every time I use the app to get into the garage.

Somewhat ironically, though, our need for this tool has flipped. Now we live in a very secure neighborhood -- kids leave their bikes on their front lawns, etc -- so the "yell at me if I leave it open" function isn't as important. OTOH, since I haven't been able to find a suitable garage door opener that will mount cleanly on my motorcycles, using the phone to get into the garage has become the default.

Chalk me up to another happy user of Ratgdo. I got one of the older ESP8266-based ones whose Homekit firmware has been in "maintenance mode" by the developer due to its board having limited RAM and processing power to do the things they're doing with the current boards. That was a bummer to find out since I'd had the thing for less than a year and I was using the "dry contact" system: manually wired magnetic switches on the door to tell the board whether the door is up, down, or in a state between (opening or closing). It's a very, very old garage door opener.

Since the code was put in a "best-effort basis" for future updates, it's gone from version 2.2 to 2.2.6 with numerous fixes. Most notable was software-configurable "debounce" functionality which finally solved my problem with the door tripping the magnetic reed switches several times quickly when the door comes to a stop and confusing the board about its current up/down status.

I bring it up because I have tremendous enthusiasm for people who take an idea, a cheap microcontroller, and put together a solution for people who prefer to stick with older, simple appliances but still want some sort of smart functionality. People who "make cool stuff and put it on the internet." That the creator disclosed that he's putting his focus on the newer boards and will maintain/fix issues with the older ones on a "best-effort" and then actually does it... it's fantastic. Because of this continued support and fixes, I can't recommend Ratgdo boards enough.

Had the same issue (the original ratgdo being unstable) and I finally just got the ratgdo32 and it's been working beautifully with HomeKit.

I wonder if someone will try to use AI to optimize the 8266 version to better handle RAM etc.
For those curious, the apparent character-spam "RATGDO" is actually an acronym for Rage Against The Garage Door Opener.

We say this about many things in tech, but IoT really seems like an area that's long overdue for some kind of open protocol standardization. The device makers can build their services on top of it and run whatever business model they want, but they should at least be forced to give us an escape hatch.

I have had a MyQ-enabled garage door opener for about a month now. I wanted a dumb one, but the installer company who replaced the garage door didn't offer one. Instead, it's just sitting there, denied Bluetooth and WiFi access until I get around to hooking up the z-wave dry contact relay controller (or perhaps ratgo, but I already have a spare relay sitting around).

A few weeks ago, I noticed my Apollo-1 Air quality sensor was seeing some strange behavior in the basement. Home Assistant showed an unexplained temperature spike and humidity drop a little before 1am.

I managed to figure out from other sensors that nothing was actually awry (no spikes in draw of nearby devices, no telltale gas signatures of the water heater kicking on, no motion or CO2 indicating human or other large animal presence). Was the board malfunctioning? Fortunately the device has an internal temperature sensor and an ambient sensor which are separate. Logging confirms the temperature spike originated on the board, probably from the WiFi chip.

But, why?

It turns out, after inspecting the signal a bit more, than the MyQ was broadcasting so loudly between the WiFi and BLE, screaming for someone to talk to it, that my air sensor was having to increase its power to still be able to communicate over all the noise. Switching to a different channel for the crappy old downstairs AP fixed it, but still, c'mon!

I'm a little wary of connecting any sort of ingress/egress to my home to the network at all, even locally, but an honest appraisal of the basement is that smashing a window is probably a much bigger threat model than hacking the door opener. Or in other words, https://xkcd.com/538/

A thief going into your basement by hacking your garage door may not be a realistic scenario, but your garage door being hacked and used in a botnet or intercepting your traffic and injecting malware into it is very much a thing that may happen.
